description: Sentence Improvement is a crucial topic where grammatical or structural flaws in the underlined part of a given sentence must be identified and replaced with the correct option. It tests the understanding of grammar, vocabulary, and syntax.

sections.title: Basic Concept and Strategy
sections.description: Adopting the right approach is essential to accurately solve Sentence Improvement questions.

key_concepts.explanation: Carefully read the underlined part of the sentence and identify if the error lies in grammar, tense, or vocabulary.

strategies.title: Understand the Context
strategies.detail: Read the whole sentence, not just the underlined part, to make the overall meaning clear.

strategies.title: Elimination Method
strategies.detail: Eliminate options that are grammatically incorrect or change the meaning of the original sentence.

strategies.title: No Improvement
strategies.detail: If the original sentence is already correct according to grammar and context, always choose the 'No Improvement' option.

sections.title: Subject-Verb Agreement Rules
sections.description: The verb in a sentence must always agree with its subject in number and person.

grammar_rules.explanation: The form of the verb is strictly determined by the subject.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The list of items are on the desk.
examples.correct_or_usage: The list of items is on the desk.
examples.explanation: Here, the main subject 'list' is singular, not 'items', so the singular verb 'is' will be used.

exceptions.explanation: 'A number of' is always followed by a plural verb, while 'The number of' takes a singular verb.
exceptions.example: A number of students are present. / The number of students is fifty.

sections.title: Tense and Conditional Sentences
sections.description: The correct context of time and the proper structure of conditions are essential in sentences.

grammar_rules.structure: If + Subject + V1 (Simple Present), Subject + Will/Shall + V1 (Simple Future)
grammar_rules.explanation: For a future condition, the present tense is used in the 'If' clause.

examples.incorrect_or_context: If I will go to Delhi, I will meet him.
examples.correct_or_usage: If I go to Delhi, I will meet him.
examples.explanation: In conditional sentences, the future tense auxiliary 'will' is not used in the 'If' clause.

exceptions.explanation: For an unreal or imaginary situation, 'were' is always used, even with a singular subject.
exceptions.example: If I were a bird, I would fly.

sections.title: Modifiers and Parallelism
sections.description: Modifiers should be properly placed in a sentence, and there should be a balance of similar grammatical structures.

key_concepts.explanation: When two or more ideas or actions are joined by 'and', 'or', or 'but' in a sentence, their grammatical form must be identical.
A modifier must be placed right next to the word it modifies; otherwise, the meaning of the sentence becomes illogical.

examples.incorrect_or_context: She likes to read, to sing, and dancing.
examples.correct_or_usage: She likes reading, singing, and dancing.
examples.explanation: This violates the rule of parallelism. All verbs must be in the same format (e.g., gerund form).

sections.title: Prepositions and Redundancy
sections.description: Using the correct prepositions and avoiding redundant words ensures accuracy and secures marks in Sentence Improvement.

key_concepts.explanation: Using two words with the same meaning together is grammatically incorrect (a superfluous error).

examples.explanation: The meaning of 'back' is inherent in the word 'return', making the use of 'back' redundant.

exceptions.explanation: Certain verbs or adjectives are followed by a fixed preposition, which cannot be changed or omitted.
exceptions.example: He is addicted to smoking. (Here, using V1+ing after 'to' is a standard exception to the infinitive rule).
